content: The Consolidated Guidelines on Person-Centred HIV Patient Monitoring and Case Surveillance, published by the World Health Organization (WHO) in June 2017, provide comprehensive recommendations for improving HIV monitoring systems. These guidelines emphasize a person-centred approach to HIV care, focusing on the use of unique patient identifiers to link individuals across various health services. This approach aims to enhance the continuity of care, improve patient outcomes, and support public health surveillance efforts. The guidelines outline the importance of integrating HIV patient monitoring with broader health care needs, such as tuberculosis (TB), maternal and child health (MCH), and other chronic conditions. This includes tracking sentinel events, such as HIV diagnosis, initiation of antiretroviral therapy (ART), viral load testing, and patient outcomes like retention in care and viral suppression. The document also highlights the critical role of data security and confidentiality in patient monitoring systems. The guidelines advocate for transitioning from paper-based to electronic health information systems to enable better data disaggregation by time, person, and place, and to improve the overall efficiency of health information management. The overarching goal of these guidelines is to support countries in implementing the treat all approach and achieving the global 90-90-90 HIV targets by 2020. These targets aim for 90% of people living with HIV to know their status, 90% of those diagnosed to receive ART, and 90% of those on treatment to achieve viral suppression. The guidelines also align with the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), promoting person-centred development and ensuring no one is left behind. To achieve these objectives, the guidelines recommend strengthening patient-level monitoring systems, expanding HIV case surveillance, and investing in unique patient identifiers to link individual records across facilities and programs. They also emphasize the importance of conducting a comprehensive situation analysis before implementing these systems, ensuring that they are tailored to national needs and priorities. The guidelines were developed through extensive consultations with technical experts, national AIDS program staff, and representatives from various countries and organizations. They are intended for use by national and subnational HIV program managers, surveillance officers, and other personnel involved in designing and implementing monitoring and evaluation systems. Additionally, they provide valuable insights for technical partners and stakeholders supporting HIV health sector programs. In summary, these guidelines aim to improve the quality and sustainability of HIV care by promoting integrated, person-centred monitoring systems that link patients to comprehensive health services while ensuring data security and confidentiality.
